title: A Pulsating Liver and Swollen Legs / The Liver Is Telling You About the Heart

blocks.text: A Pulsating Liver and Swollen Legs / The Liver Is Telling You About the Heart

AMaC MRCP PACES · R2-09 · Physical examination · PACES Station 4, abdominal examination encounter · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 min: up to 6 min examining, then at least 4 min of examiner questions · Guidelines: ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease (published 29 August 2025); NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation (published 27 April 2021; last updated 30 June 2021) · Related AMaC: Abdominal examination: chronic liver disease; splenomegaly. Cardiovascular examination: tricuspid regurgitation (the same valve lesion examined from the heart; link when that station is published)

Mr Leonard Yates, 71, a retired farmer, has had swollen ankles and a full, aching abdomen for three months. Please examine his abdomen to establish the cause. You have up to 6 minutes to examine, followed by questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A tender, smooth liver that pulses with each heartbeat, with a raised neck vein, means tricuspid regurgitation and right heart failure, not liver disease.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates find the big liver and ascites and call it cirrhosis, never looking at the neck or the heart. Pass: feel the pulsation, examine the JVP and listen for the murmur. Fail: a liver diagnosis without the neck. Pass behaviour includes asking before pressing on a tender liver.

rows: A tender liver needs care; look at the whole patient.
"Mr Yates, may I examine your tummy? Tell me if it is sore."
Introduce, consent, ask about pain, sit at 45 degrees, expose; look at neck veins, legs and abdomen.
Is the liver pulsatile, and is there fluid?
"I'll press gently over the liver. Tell me if it hurts."
Palpate liver edge and expansile pulsation; percuss; shifting dullness; oedema.
Link the liver to the neck and the heart.
"I'd like to look at your neck veins and listen to your heart."
JVP and v waves, ear lobe movement, pulse rhythm, left sternal edge murmur louder on inspiration.
Name the cause and what to do next.
"This is tricuspid regurgitation with right heart failure. I'd arrange an echocardiogram."
Cover him, thank him; present findings, causes, plan.
Presses hard on a tender liver; no pain question
Introduces, obtains consent, cleans hands, asks about pain, palpates gently, covers him
Offers a chaperone; sits him up for comfort and stops if he winces
Abdomen only; no neck or heart examination
Palpates the liver gently; checks JVP, pulse and auscultation
Notes expansile pulsation and ear lobe movement; auscultates in inspiration
Reports stigmata of chronic liver disease that are absent
Tender pulsatile liver, ascites, oedema, raised JVP, irregular pulse, systolic murmur
Adds giant v waves and a murmur louder in inspiration; no spider naevi, no jaundice
Tricuspid regurgitation with right heart failure
Tricuspid regurgitation with congestive hepatopathy; AF and annular dilatation may contribute, until echocardiography assesses the mechanism
Names pulmonary hypertension or left heart disease
Adds atrial fibrillation, rheumatic disease and endocarditis, with reasons
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): asks for a percutaneous liver biopsy.
Echocardiogram, ECG, liver tests, kidney function
Adds natriuretic peptide and lung assessment for pulmonary hypertension
No treatment for fluid; liver clinic only
Diuretic per local protocol; treat the cause; cardiology referral
Names rate control, kidney monitoring and valve intervention per specialist decision

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. High-performance includes the pass behaviours. This station-specific grid is an AMaC teaching framework mapped to PACES skills, not an official mark scheme. Consent, hand hygiene, dignity and an appropriate chaperone are baseline professional practice. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type: the patient is a real or simulated patient and the findings are in section 8.

Findings (released as each step is done). Pulse 88, irregularly irregular; BP 118/70 (scenario values). JVP raised to the jaw at 45 degrees with giant systolic v waves; ear lobe movement. Pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge, louder on inspiration. Liver edge 4 cm below the costal margin, smooth, tender, pulsatile; ascites; oedema to the knees. No jaundice or spider naevi.

Question ladder. Q1 Findings and diagnosis (R3, R4): tricuspid regurgitation with right heart failure. Q2 Cause (R5): pulmonary hypertension, left heart disease, atrial fibrillation with annular dilatation, rheumatic disease, endocarditis. Q3 Investigations (R6): echocardiogram, ECG, liver and kidney tests. Q4 Management (R7): diuretic per local protocol, treat the cause, specialist valve review (ESC/EACTS 2025).

Normal-findings variant for a separate teaching exercise. No pulsatile liver, normal JVP. The candidate must say the abdomen is normal. Do not switch the defined case to this variant during the encounter.
Curveball 1. "Is this cirrhosis?" Safe: cardiac congestion is favoured by pulsatility, raised JVP and murmur; cirrhosis may coexist and is not excluded by absent stigmata.
Curveball 2. "He is breathless lying flat." Safe: sit him up and assess for heart failure; urgent review.
Curveball 3. "Would you biopsy the liver?" Safe: no; it is congested and the cause is cardiac.
Introduces, consents and asks about pain before pressing (G)
Palpates gently and feels expansile pulsation (A)
Examines JVP and describes the waveform (A)
Listens for a murmur louder on inspiration (A)
Reports tender pulsatile liver, ascites and oedema (B)
Reports irregular pulse and raised JVP (B)
Names tricuspid regurgitation with right heart failure (D)
Gives causes (D)
Requests an echocardiogram (E)
Suggests a diuretic and cardiology referral (E)
Fail performance
(Presses hard on the liver and does not ask about pain. [R1 Fail] Does not examine the neck or heart. [R2 Fail])
CANDIDATE: He has spider naevi and jaundice. [R3 Fail] This is cirrhosis. [R4 Fail] I don't know the cause. [R5 Fail]
EXAMINER: What would you do?
CANDIDATE: A liver biopsy. [R6 Fail] A hepatology clinic. [R7 Fail]

Examiner note: No pain check, signs invented, neck and heart ignored, and a liver biopsy requested, which is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): a congested liver with ascites is a bleeding risk and the cause is cardiac.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello Mr Yates, I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your tummy? Is it sore? Tell me if it hurts. [R1 Pass]
(Sits him up, palpates the liver gently, checks the JVP and pulse, then auscultates. [R2 Pass])
CANDIDATE: The liver is tender and pulsatile with ascites and oedema; the JVP is raised, the pulse irregular and there is a systolic murmur. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: This is tricuspid regurgitation with right heart failure. [R4 Pass] It may be from pulmonary hypertension or left heart disease. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Thank you, Mr Yates. I'll cover you. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: How would you investigate?
CANDIDATE: An echocardiogram, ECG, liver and kidney tests. [R6 Pass]
EXAMINER: And management?
CANDIDATE: A diuretic per local protocol, treat the cause, and refer to cardiology. [R7 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and accurate. Did not describe giant v waves or name atrial fibrillation.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello Mr Yates, I'm one of the doctors. May I examine your tummy? Is it sore? Tell me if it hurts. [R1 High]
(Sits him up, palpates the liver gently, checks the JVP and pulse, then auscultates. [R2 High])
CANDIDATE: May I offer a chaperone? I'll sit you up and stop if it hurts. [R1 High]
(Feels expansile pulsation, sees ear lobe movement, auscultates in inspiration. [R2 High])
CANDIDATE: Giant v waves, a murmur louder on inspiration, a tender pulsatile liver, ascites. No spider naevi or jaundice. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Tricuspid regurgitation with congestive hepatopathy. AF may contribute to annular dilatation; echocardiography will assess the mechanism. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: Causes include pulmonary hypertension, atrial fibrillation, rheumatic disease and endocarditis. [R5 High]
EXAMINER: How would you investigate?
CANDIDATE: Echocardiogram, natriuretic peptide, ECG, kidney function and lung assessment. [R6 High]
EXAMINER: And management?
CANDIDATE: A diuretic with kidney monitoring, assessment of AF including stroke prevention, rate treatment if needed, and specialist valve review. [R7 High]
Examiner note: Linked liver, neck and heart and named the cause.
R2: Examining the abdomen alone misses the neck vein and murmur that explain the liver.
R3: Reporting spider naevi or jaundice that are absent points to the wrong diagnosis.
R4: Calling it cirrhosis ignores the pulsation and raised JVP.
R6: A liver biopsy in a congested liver with ascites targets the wrong organ and risks bleeding.
R1: Pressing hard on a tender liver without asking is a welfare failure.
"Let me look at the neck veins."
"A pulsatile liver means the heart."
"I'd start with an echocardiogram."
Tricuspid regurgitation: giant systolic v waves, pulsatile liver, pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge louder on inspiration.
Right heart failure causes tender hepatomegaly, ascites and oedema.
Most tricuspid regurgitation is secondary to left heart disease, pulmonary hypertension or atrial fibrillation; echocardiography grades it (ESC/EACTS 2025).

Assess tricuspid regurgitation and right ventricular function with echocardiography. Use diuretics with renal and electrolyte monitoring for congestion; review the cause and specialist valve options. Confirm AF with ECG and assess stroke and bleeding risk. Liver disease can coexist with cardiac congestion.
THINK: Right heart failure; kidney injury from diuresis.
SAY: "Tricuspid regurgitation with right heart failure."
DO: Ask about pain; gentle palpation; neck; heart.
NUMBERS: Pulse 88, BP 118/70 (scenario values).
TRAP: Calling it cirrhosis.
FINISH: Echocardiogram, diuretic per protocol, cardiology.
